Andy Whitman Swan's Island LD 1231
My name is Andy Whitman, of Swan's Island, Maine, an island community served by the Maine State Ferry Service (MSFS). I'm providing testimony today in support of requiring MSFS ferries to be overnighted on the islands they serve. The DoT and MSFS are proposing to overnight ferries on the mainland which will drastically impact island communities and their livelihoods.
First, this change would eliminate a critical round trip each day. Ferries starting and ending their day on the island ensure that residents can travel to and from the mainland in the early morning and late afternoon. Overnighting ferries on the mainland means the first trip to the island becomes positioning, not passenger service--stranding residents without early access to work, school, medical care, or connecting transport. On Swan's Island, this means an 1.5 hours off island every day is lost, making off island employment near impossible, and access to medical care incredibly difficult. Furthermore, students and their families already struggle to go to school and enjoy extra-curricular activities without added burden of staying off island or arranging other transportation. Overnighting the state ferry on the mainland only exacerbates this issue.
Second, this change would undermine the ferry's role as a lifeline during emergencies. When ferries are docked at the island overnight, they are available to transport emergency personnel, evacuate patients, and respond to critical needs. Without that presence, island residents lose precious response time in situations where every minute matters.
This proposal prioritizes operational convenience over community safety and access. The state's ferries are not just transportation--they are infrastructure, emergency response, and daily life support for islanders. Please preserve their commitment to the communities they exist to serve.

Good afternoon, Senator Nangle, Representative Crafts, and members of the Joint Committee on
Transportation. Thank you for the opportunity to testify today. My name is Representative Billy Bob
Faulkingham, and I serve as the House Republican Leader. I represent House District 12, which includes the towns of Franklin, Gouldsboro, Hancock, Sorrento, Sullivan, Winter Harbor, and Steuben.
l am here today to present testimony on my proposed legislation, LD 1231, An Act Requiring Ferries
to Dock Overnight on Certain Islands for Emergency Purposes.
This bill directs the Department of Transportation to require the Maine State Ferry Service to nightly dock a ferry vessel that carries vehicles overnight in the towns of Swan's island, Vinalhaven, North Haven, and lslesboro, to ensure availability for emergency medical, fire, and law enforcement needs, as well as for mass evacuation purposes if needed.
Maine's island communities are unique, and their residents are known for being independent,
resilient, and resourceful. However, like all communities, they deserve equal access to essential services that help protect public safety and health, especially in times of crisis. Currently, island residents rely heavily on ferry services to connect them to the mainland for essential medical services, to conduct business, and to ensure public safety. However, there are limitations during
emergencies when timely access to services is most critical.
On the islands of Swan's Island, Vinalhaven, North Haven, and lslesboro, residents often face significant delays when seeking emergency medical care. The delays in ferry service can be life-
threatening, particularly for patients requiring urgent care or transport to hospitals on the mainland. The proposed legislation would address this by ensuring that ferry services are available around the
clock, enabling emergency vehicles to be transported efficiently to and from the islands when the
need arises, particularly for critical care such as heart attacks, strokes, and trauma injuries.
Island communities often face heightened risks in the event of fire outbreaks or law enforcement emergencies due to limited resources and delayed responses from the mainland. For example, a 2017 fire on Vinalhaven resulted in a delay of nearly three hours for essential firefighting equipment to be transported by ferry from the mainland. This delay could have been mitigated if the ferry service had docked overnight, enabling quicker mobilization of emergency response teams.
While we hope never to face a natural disaster or emergency that would require mass evacuation, it
is essential to be prepared. These Islands are particularly vulnerable to being cut off from the mainland during severe weather, and delays in ferry access can significantly impede timely evacuation in cases of fires, storms, or other disaster situations.

In conclusion, LD 1231, "An Act Requiring Ferries to Dock Overnight on Certain Islands for
Emergency Purposes," will ensure that the residents of Swan's island, Vinalhaven, North Haven, and lslesboro are afforded the same access to emergency services that mainland residents enjoy. This bill will save lives, provide essential services more efficiently, and make sure our island communities are equipped with the tools they need to handle emergencies swiftly and safely.
l ask for your support in advancing this important legislation to safeguard the health, safety, and well being of Maine's island residents. Thank you for your time and consideration.

Senator Nangle, Representative Crafts, and Distinguished Members of the Committee on Transportation, I am Gabriel Pendleton, I am a resident of Islesboro, alternate member for Islesboro on the Ferry Service Advisory Board, and regular rider on the Maine State Ferry Service trip between Lincolnville and Islesboro. I write now to express my support for LDs 1231 and 947 which seek to clarify the nighttime berthing location of certain MSFS ferries including the Islesboro ferry.
DOT Commissioner Bruce Van Note has expressed his desire to have ferries remain on the mainland at night. For reference, currently the Islesboro ferry is berthed on the island from 5:30PM until 7:30AM the next morning. The Commissioner's stated goal with this policy is to retain and hire new crew members. This is undoubtedly a laudable goal which all Islands support. However, shortly after the Commissioner expressed support for this policy the union that represents our ferry crews took a poll among active crew members and more than half would quit if this policy were implemented, please see the attached survey.
Staffing issues aside, there are other concerns about berthing ferries away from their island ports. Representatives from my community's EMS, Fire, and Public Safety departments have expressed concern about changes to emergency response protocols and potential delays if boats are berthed off island. Examples of emergency situations which require ferry trips include: mutual aid fire trucks coming to respond to a large fire; forestry equipment to fight a forest fire; State or Federal law enforcement to respond to a myriad of public safety emergencies; ambulances and medical staff needed to respond to a mass casualty event. Further, concerns about berthing location are different for each island served by the MSFS as some are further away from their mainland port, some have two boats, some have less protected harbors, etc.
All that is to say, the decision to change the berthing locations of ferries is not as simple as it sounds and should not be taken lightly. The impact of such a policy change should be made as part of a major substantive rule change after careful consideration and input from all islands and other stakeholders. This will achieve better policy and community buy in from the islands.
Thank you for your consideration.

The biggest ferry news this year on North Haven and every single other island served by the Maine State Ferry Service, is the DOT's proposal to have the ferries spend the night on the mainland to theoretically save money...a radical idea which would mark the end of decades (from the beginning) of the ferries overnighting on their respective islands. It would change island life dramatically for the worse, beginning with the schedule. It would negatively affect all parts of island life and every facet of our town, from the school which sends students to Region 8 on a tight schedule, the store with tightly scheduled freight runs, construction crews, town office, post office, boatyards, auto repairs, and simply going to Rockland for the day or afternoon to pick up medicine or supplies, or maybe have fun.
The single most dangerous outcome to having the ferry overnight on the mainland would be removing it as our `emergency medical boat', capable of taking a patient in the ambulance at night to Pen-Bay Hospital, a function it has served since the inception of the Ferry Service. There are times when it is medically necessary to keep a patient in the ambulance and not trundling them down a steep ramp to an icy float. The alternatives offered by the ferry service fall far short compared to having the ferry ready to sail, berthed on island overnight, most crucially the alternative emergence transport boats are not able to accommodate the ambulance. North Haven's EMS crew made a terrific short video documenting the risks of taking a patient down the ramp to the

town float to a waiting lobster boat for transport. It's on You-tube listed as `EMS Transport Movie', directed by Courtney Naliboff.
We have, again, been extremely fortunate in our captains and crews being very willing to make these late night trips. If we lose this emergency transport by ambulance as part of the Ferry Service, our lives will be placed at risk.
Crew work-life balance is also touted as an advantage for ferry crew by basing our boat in Rockland, though not a concept universally shared by the crew. More than half of those questioned would not be able to continue in their job if required to commute daily to Rockland to serve on the `North Haven route'. Presently, crew members are fine with a weekly commute from over an hour away for many. To make the same commute daily would not be practical or safe, or perhaps even allowed.
It's hard to believe that overnighting on the mainland would save the DOT money in today's real estate market with having to build/buy crew housing at every mainland ferry destination (Rockland, Lincolnville, Mount Desert). For our route, requiring crew to live near Rockland for commuting purposes would potentially make it harder to find enough crew than it is now.
In order to have a ferry safely overnight in Lincolnville, it's thought that a breakwater would need to be built, at a cost likely in the millions of dollars. The seas can build dangerously high at that ferry landing in a southerly blow, placing both the ferry and the ferry pen at risk.

In our case, we would have to wait for the boat to arrive from Rockland every morning before we could leave North Haven for the mainland. Our day would be delayed by well over an hour, making it impossible to get to a Portland medical appointment and back in time for the late boat (at whatever time that might be). For that matter, would we arrive in Rockland in time to have a useful day there? Alternatively, the Ferry Service has floated one idea of having the Vinalhaven morning boat come up here to pick up passengers and vehicles before heading to Rockland...a real non-starter for both North Haven and Vinalhaven. We would be asked to rely upon our neighboring island which has experienced the most difficulty in fully crewing their boats, resulting in the worst reliability percentage of all the islands. Vinalhaven would probably not want to give up space on its already full morning boat. At the end of the day, would there be time for the return trip with the crew to Rockland and still keep within the Coast Guard's 12 hour work limit? Would we still have three trips per day? So far, no answers to these questions.
More than at any other time, all the islands are organized and together in opposing this ill conceived and damaging idea. There have been numerous Zoom call meetings by island representatives among the islands served by the MSFS and a number of bills are being presented to the Legislature to counter this proposal. There is hope that we may avoid this poorly thought out concept.
